rows.question: What is the main claim of this piece, and where is it argued?
rows.text:
The piece's central claim is that most published research findings are false, and that this can be proven rather than just suspected [spya-xpu5tw]. The author states plainly that it can be proven that most claimed research findings are false [spya-zjrg6r].

The argument runs in stages through the article:

- It starts by building a mathematical model: the chance a finding is true (the "positive predictive value") depends on the study's statistical power, its significance threshold, and crucially the pre-study odds that the relationship being tested is real at all [spya-hjja9x].
- It then adds two real-world distortions to that model — bias in how studies are designed, analyzed and reported [spya-j7femp, spya-s46ctb], and the effect of many independent teams all testing the same question [spya-zjre9m, spya-u5x4p2].
- From this model it draws six corollaries about when findings are less likely to be true: smaller studies, smaller effect sizes, more and less-selected hypotheses tested, more design flexibility, stronger financial/other interests, and "hotter" fields with more competing teams [spya-nx5jjr, spya-vzv8aq, spya-p2upz7, spya-f65pfg, spya-hkh8ey, spya-s4b0q7, spya-mgrr58].
- It backs this with worked simulations across study types, showing a positive predictive value above 50% is hard to achieve in most designs [spya-j5xgg2, spya-umhdpk], and a numeric example of a genome-wide schizophrenia study [spya-c5mfye, spya-y0a3ah, spya-uvmvbc].
- It closes by arguing that in fields with no real effects at all, published "findings" may just be accurate measurements of the field's bias [spya-pw5xz4, spya-khfp04, spya-x7m59a], and offers suggestions for improving the situation [spya-t4k903].

rows.question: What does the paragraph beginning “Corollary 1: The smaller the studies conducted in a scientific” mean?
rows.text:
This paragraph (Corollary 1) says that smaller studies are less likely to produce true findings, because a smaller sample size gives less statistical power, and lower power pushes the probability that a positive result is actually true (the paper's "PPV") down toward the point where a finding is only as likely true as a coin flip, roughly whenever power drops to 0.05 or lower [spya-vzv8aq].

It then gives a comparison: fields that run large studies, like heart-disease trials with several thousand randomized patients, are more trustworthy than fields built on much smaller studies, such as most research into molecular predictors, where sample sizes can be about a hundred times smaller [spya-vzv8aq].

rows.question: Which paragraph gives the strongest support for the central claim, going only on the piece itself?
rows.text:
My inference is that the paragraph giving the strongest support is the one summarizing the Table 4 simulations, since it moves from the abstract formulas to concrete, concrete numbers across real research situations. It states that in this framework, a PPV (positive predictive value — the chance a claimed finding is actually true) exceeding 50% is hard to achieve, and works through specific cases: a well-powered randomized trial starting at 50% pre-study odds is true about 85% of the time, but underpowered early-phase trials are true only about one in four times, and discovery-oriented research with massive testing (such as testing thousands of genes at once) has extremely low PPV even with good methodological standards [spya-umhdpk].

This paragraph is the strongest support, in my reading, because it is where the earlier formulas (power, bias, number of competing teams) are actually applied to realistic research settings and yield numbers — rather than staying at the level of algebra — making the "most findings are false" claim concrete and checkable rather than asserted.

rows.question: What does the author mean by positive predictive value?
rows.text:
In this piece, positive predictive value (PPV) is the probability that a research finding is actually true, given that it has already been reported as statistically significant [spya-hjja9x]. The article sets this up with a 2×2 table comparing what studies claim against the real, "gold standard" relationships in a field, and PPV is the post-study probability of truth you get once you plug in the field's pre-study odds, the study's statistical power, and the significance threshold [spya-hjja9x].

The article also notes that PPV is the flip side of what another paper calls the false positive report probability: PPV is "the complementary probability of what Wacholder et al. have called the false positive report probability" [spya-hjja9x].

For context, the term comes from diagnostic testing more broadly — outside this piece, PPV is a standard statistics term for the share of positive test results that are true positives, and Ioannidis is repurposing that same idea here to ask, of all "significant" research results, what share are actually true relationships.

rows.question: What is the main claim of this piece, and where is it argued?
rows.text:
The main claim is that most published research findings are false, and this follows as a logical/mathematical consequence of how statistical significance works combined with bias and study design — not just an empirical observation [spya-xpu5tw spya-zjrg6r].

The argument runs in stages:

- It first builds a model using a 2×2 table comparing claimed findings to true relationships, deriving a formula for the "positive predictive value" (PPV) — the probability a statistically significant finding is actually true — based on study power, significance threshold, and the ratio of true to false relationships being tested in a field [spya-hjja9x].
- It then extends that model to add bias (design, analysis, and reporting choices that manufacture positive results) and to account for multiple independent teams testing the same question, both of which drive PPV down further [spya-j7femp spya-zjre9m].
- From this it draws six corollaries: findings are less likely true in fields with small studies, small effect sizes, more and less-selected tested relationships, more flexibility in design/analysis, stronger financial or other interests, and more competing teams [spya-nx5jjr].
- It then runs simulations across realistic research scenarios showing PPV rarely exceeds 50% [spya-j5xgg2 spya-umhdpk], and argues that in fields with no true effects at all, claimed findings simply measure the prevailing bias [spya-pw5xz4 spya-x7m59a].
- It closes by proposing ways to improve the situation, such as better-powered studies, registration, and more honest acknowledgment of pre-study odds [spya-t4k903 spya-a2jbw9 spya-fa6b0w spya-mjwvkp].

rows.question: What does the final paragraph of the article say?
rows.text:
The final paragraph argues that most new discoveries will keep coming from hypothesis-generating research with low or very low pre-study odds, so a single study's statistical significance only gives a partial picture without knowing how much testing happened elsewhere in the field. It adds that even with the large statistical literature on multiple testing corrections, it's usually impossible to know how much data dredging preceded a finding, and that even knowing this wouldn't reveal the pre-study odds anyway — so researchers must make subjective but still useful assumptions about how many tested relationships are likely true [spya-y44q7p].

rows.question: What is the main claim of this piece, and where is it argued?
rows.text:
The main claim is that people can't think clearly about anything that's become part of their identity, so the best strategy is to keep as few things in your identity as possible, since fewer labels make for clearer thought [spya-xv45wq spya-nt9xpg].

The argument builds in stages. It starts by noting that religion and politics produce uniquely bad discussions, and traces this to the fact that with those topics no expertise threshold is needed—only strong conviction [spya-pfruy3 spya-dpvyy2]. It then locates the real cause not in the topics themselves but in identity: discussions turn bad once they're "driven mostly by people's identities," which is why a Bronze Age battle can be discussed calmly while a modern one can't [spya-kwzcxp spya-uz3ta2]. This is generalized with the programming-language example, showing identity (not the topic's nature) decides whether a question can be reasoned about, even on questions with real answers [spya-s6tp4k spya-zdmhnz]. From there the piece draws its practical conclusion about shrinking your identity [spya-xv45wq], with a closing note that even useful-seeming identities like "scientist" work only because they don't commit you to any fixed belief [spya-mz9mzj].

rows.question: What does the paragraph beginning “More generally, you can have a fruitful discussion about a” mean?
rows.text:
This paragraph generalizes the point just made about programming languages: a topic only becomes impossible to discuss sensibly when it is tied to someone's sense of who they are, not because of anything about the topic itself [spya-zdmhnz].

The article states that politics and religion are especially dangerous only because they happen to be tied to many people's identities, not because they are inherently different from other subjects — and that in principle you could still have a useful conversation about them with people who don't identify with a side [spya-zdmhnz]. It then gives the reverse case: something as ordinary as arguing over Ford versus Chevy trucks can be just as unsafe to discuss, if the people involved have made "Ford guy" or "Chevy guy" part of who they are [spya-zdmhnz].

My inference is that the paragraph's function in the argument is to detach "topics to avoid" from any fixed list — it's not that religion, politics, or trucks are special categories, but that *any* topic becomes a minefield once it's wrapped up in identity, which sets up the next paragraph's advice to keep as few things in your identity as possible.
